name: Dublin
summary: The Irish capital that anchors the fiction of James Joyce.
significance: Joyce set Ulysses on a single day, 16 June 1904, and Dubliners across the city's streets, pubs and parlours. Bloomsday walkers still follow Leopold Bloom's route.

name: Sweny's Pharmacy
summary: A preserved Victorian chemist where Leopold Bloom buys lemon soap.
significance: The shop is named in the Lotus Eaters episode of Ulysses. It now runs as a volunteer-staffed shop and reading room.

name: James Joyce Tower and Museum
q: James Joyce Tower and Museum, Sandycove
summary: The Martello tower that opens Ulysses, now a museum.
significance: Joyce stayed here briefly in 1904. The novel's first scene takes place on its roof, making it both a story setting and a museum.

name: James Joyce Centre
q: James Joyce Centre, North Great George's Street, Dublin
summary: A Georgian townhouse dedicated to Joyce's life and work.
significance: A literary institution with exhibitions, talks and walking tours on Joyce's Dublin.

name: The Plaza Hotel
q: The Plaza Hotel, Fifth Avenue, New York
summary: The Fifth Avenue hotel where the tension in The Great Gatsby boils over.
significance: The confrontation between Gatsby and Tom Buchanan takes place in a suite at the Plaza on a hot summer afternoon.

name: Great Neck, Long Island
summary: The North Shore peninsula widely seen as the model for West Egg.
significance: Fitzgerald lived in Great Neck while writing the novel. West Egg itself is fictional, so the link is inspiration rather than a named setting.

name: Jane Austen's House
summary: The Hampshire cottage where Austen revised her major novels.
significance: Austen lived here from 1809 to 1817 and prepared Pride and Prejudice for publication and wrote Persuasion in this period.

name: Bath
summary: The Georgian spa city at the centre of Persuasion's later chapters.
significance: Anne Elliot's family relocates to Bath, and its streets and assembly rooms frame the novel's social world.

name: Jane Austen Centre
q: Jane Austen Centre, Gay Street, Bath
summary: A museum about Austen's time in Bath.
significance: Austen lived in Bath between 1801 and 1806. The centre explores how the city shaped Persuasion and Northanger Abbey.

name: The Cobb, Lyme Regis
summary: A curved stone harbour wall and the scene of Louisa Musgrove's fall.
significance: In Persuasion, Louisa's jump from the Cobb steps changes the course of the plot.

name: Paris
summary: The French capital behind Les Misérables and A Moveable Feast.
significance: Hugo's novel traces the city's streets and uprisings, and Hemingway's memoir recalls his 1920s years in its cafés and bookshops.

name: Maison de Victor Hugo
q: Maison de Victor Hugo, Place des Vosges, Paris
summary: Hugo's former apartment on the Place des Vosges.
significance: Hugo lived here from 1832 to 1848 and began work on the book that became Les Misérables during that period.

name: Shakespeare and Company
q: Shakespeare and Company, Rue de la Bûcherie, Paris
summary: An English-language bookshop facing Notre-Dame on the Left Bank.
significance: The original shop, run by Sylvia Beach, lent books to Hemingway and published Ulysses. The present shop opened in 1951 as Le Mistral and took its name in 1964.

name: La Closerie des Lilas
q: La Closerie des Lilas, Boulevard du Montparnasse, Paris
summary: A Montparnasse brasserie Hemingway used as an outdoor study.
significance: A Moveable Feast describes writing at this café, and the brasserie keeps the tradition alive.

name: Sherlock Holmes Museum, Baker Street
q: Sherlock Holmes Museum, Baker Street, London
summary: A museum that presents itself as the home of the detective at 221B.
significance: Conan Doyle gave Holmes the address 221B Baker Street, which did not exist when written. The museum sits between numbers 237 and 241 and displays the 221B sign by permission.

name: Dartmoor
summary: The Devon moorland where The Hound of the Baskervilles unfolds.
significance: Doyle named the real moor as the book's setting and drew on local legend and the surrounding landscape for its atmosphere.

name: King's Cross Station
summary: The London terminus where Harry boards the Hogwarts Express.
significance: The book places Platform 9¾ here. A luggage trolley installation marks the spot, though the platform is imagined.

name: Aracataca
summary: The Colombian town where García Márquez was born.
significance: Macondo is fictional. Critics and the author himself link it to Aracataca, so treat the connection as inspiration.

name: Barcelona
summary: The Catalan city where The Shadow of the Wind takes place.
significance: Zafón follows Daniel Sempere through the Gothic Quarter and Eixample in the years after the Spanish Civil War.

name: Tokyo
summary: The city where Toru Watanabe studies and falls in love in Norwegian Wood.
significance: Murakami set the novel's late-1960s university scenes in Tokyo, against student protests and loneliness.

name: Sacra di San Michele
q: Sacra di San Michele, Piedmont, Italy
summary: A hilltop abbey often cited as an inspiration for the novel's monastery.
significance: Eco's abbey is fictional. The Sacra di San Michele is frequently mentioned as one inspiration, though the author did not name one site.

name: Windmills of Campo de Criptana
q: Molinos de viento, Campo de Criptana
summary: A ridge of historic windmills in La Mancha.
significance: Local tradition identifies these windmills with the giants Don Quixote attacks. Cervantes does not name the exact site.

name: Pamplona
summary: The Navarrese city and its fiesta in The Sun Also Rises.
significance: Hemingway's characters travel to Pamplona for the Festival of San Fermín, the novel's central set piece.

name: Café Iruña
q: Café Iruña, Plaza del Castillo, Pamplona
summary: A belle époque café on the Plaza del Castillo.
significance: Hemingway was a regular on his visits to Pamplona. The novel does not name the café, so the link is to the author rather than a specific scene.

name: Green Gables Heritage Place
q: Green Gables Heritage Place, Cavendish, Prince Edward Island
summary: The farmhouse that inspired the home of Anne Shirley.
significance: Montgomery knew the farm through her cousins and drew on it and the surrounding Cavendish landscape for Avonlea.

name: Brontë Parsonage Museum
summary: The Yorkshire home of the Brontë family.
significance: Emily Brontë wrote Wuthering Heights while living here, with the moors at the back door.

name: Saint Petersburg
summary: The imperial capital Raskolnikov wanders in Crime and Punishment.
significance: Dostoevsky named real streets and districts around Sennaya Square, and readers still trace Raskolnikov's walks.

name: Dostoevsky Memorial Museum
q: Dostoevsky Museum, Kuznechny Lane, Saint Petersburg
summary: The writer's last apartment, now a museum.
significance: Dostoevsky lived here from 1878 until his death. He wrote The Brothers Karamazov here, not Crime and Punishment, so it is linked as an author site.

name: Patriarch's Ponds
summary: The Moscow park where The Master and Margarita begins.
significance: Bulgakov opens the novel here, where a stranger predicts a fatal accident. A statue of fabulist Ivan Krylov and a monument to the book stand nearby.

name: Orchard House
q: Orchard House, Lexington Road, Concord, Massachusetts
summary: The Alcott family home where Little Women was written.
significance: Louisa May Alcott wrote the novel here, and the house closely informed the March family's home.

name: Walden Pond
summary: The glacial pond where Thoreau lived in a small cabin.
significance: Walden recounts Thoreau's two years on the shore of this pond. A replica cabin and a marker show where it stood.

name: City Lights Bookstore
q: City Lights Booksellers, Columbus Avenue, San Francisco
summary: The independent bookshop and publisher at the heart of the Beat scene.
significance: City Lights published Howl and became a gathering place for Beat writers. It is not a scene in On the Road.

name: Strand Book Store
summary: A Manhattan landmark with miles of new and used books.
significance: An independent bookstore founded in 1927 and still family-owned.

name: Daunt Books, Marylebone
q: Daunt Books, Marylebone High Street, London
summary: An Edwardian bookshop that arranges travel writing by country.
significance: A well-known independent store whose travel section organises fiction and non-fiction by place.

name: Livraria Lello
summary: A neo-Gothic bookshop with a sweeping red staircase.
significance: Open since 1906, it is one of the best-known bookshops in Europe and a popular stop for readers visiting Porto.

name: Hay-on-Wye
summary: A Welsh border town known for second-hand bookshops and its literary festival.
significance: Often called the town of books, Hay hosts a major annual literature festival and dozens of shops.
